newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain steps up pressure on China over Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Britain steps up pressure on China over Hong Kong.

text.p: Britain stepped up its diplomatic offensive on Friday to press China to drop proposals to dilute Hong Kong's civil liberties after the handover in five months' time.

Hugh Davies, leader of the British delegation to the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group (JLG) responsible for transitional matters, held a two-hour meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Zhao Jihua, during which he expressed concern about the plans the British regard as legally unsound.
A Chinese-controlled committee recommended plans last weekend to scrap or amend 25 Hong Kong laws, including part of Hong Kong's Human Rights Bill, sparking protests in the British colony.
Zhao accused the British of "staging a show", and said the proposed changes would not weaken freedoms in Hong Kong after it reverts to China at midnight on June 30.
"I feel very unhappy today. The British told the press about our meeting without asking me," Zhao told reporters minutes after Davies arrived at the Chinese JLG office.
"Their purpose is to stage a show."
Davies dismissed the claims. "It's certainly not a show because we strongly believe that some of the recommendations... are actually wrong in law," he told reporters after the meeting.
"It is certainly not a show. This is a very important subject."

Hong Kong's democracy movement sprang into action on Friday, beginning a series of protests against Beijing's plans. The activists donned dunce caps to parody the zealous antics of China's Cultural Revolution red guards.

"Oppose amendment of the Bill of Rights," about 20 demonstrators chanted in the lobby of the building housing the office of post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, who will succeed British Governor Chris Patten after the handover.
"Protect freedom of assembly. Protect freedom of association," they yelled. "Human rights cannot be violated."
The Hong Kong group also called for an all-night protest outside China's de facto embassy, the Xinhua news agency.
They plan further protests over the weekend while a provisional legislature that China will install in place of the elected Legislative Council meets across the border in China.

"I don't think we can be masters of our own house," Yeung Sum, deputy leader of the Democratic Party, told reporters when asked what the latest developments boded for the autonomy that China has promised Hong Kong after the handover.
"The Chinese Communist Party is master of the house, and Mr Tung is the servant of the Chinese Communist party," he said.
Democratic Party leader Martin Lee prepared to set off on an eight-nation tour of Europe on Sunday to lobby for support for freedom and democracy in post-handover Hong Kong.
Tung defended the changes in a speech, saying they were necessary to strike "the right balance between individual rights and social order".
Tung said other states required permits for demonstrations and set limits on the overseas links of political groups, two of the changes that are worrying the pro-democracy camp.
Patten heaped scorn on the proposals, which have drawn Britain and the United States into a new diplomatic quarrel with Beijing. China has rejected their protests as "unwise".
He drew attention to pro-China politicians, now serving on China's handover committee, who had originally backed the Bill of Rights when it was debated in 1991.
"There is a difference between an about-turn and a revolving door," Patten said.
